title: Psalm 18:1–50
context: Psalm 18 is David’s long song of deliverance—also in 2 Samuel 22—sung when the LORD had saved him from all his enemies and from Saul. He opens with whole-souled love to the LORD his strength, heaps names of refuge, and recalls cords of death and torrents of destruction that drove him to cry until God heard from his temple. Then a theophany: earth quaking, heavens bowed, cherub and wind, darkness and hail, thunder, arrows, and foundations laid bare, until God draws him from many waters, rescues him from foes too mighty, and brings him into a broad place because he delighted in him. David pleads righteousness and clean hands in the controversy, kept ways and statutes, blamelessness kept from guilt; God shows himself merciful to the merciful and opposes the crooked, saves the humble, lights the lamp, and proves a perfect way and true word as shield for all who take refuge. Equipped and trained, shielded by salvation and gentleness, he pursues and consumes enemies who cry in vain to the LORD, is made head of nations, and ends blessing the living rock, praising among the nations, and confessing great salvation and forever steadfast love to the anointed, to David and to his offspring, and above all to the Messiah.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Psalm 18:1–50.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named.

arminian.quote: David triumphs in God, praises him for past deliverances, takes comfort of his integrity which God had cleared, gives God the glory of all his victories, and expresses hope of what God would do farther. This psalm, with small variations, is written in 2 Samuel 22; composed toward the end of his life after deliverance from all enemies and from Saul. Servant—who esteems it greater honor to be thy servant than king of Israel. Love—most affectionately, and with my whole soul. Rock—to which I flee for refuge; horn—strength as in beasts whose force is in their horns. Death—dangerous troubles; floods—violent assaults like a flood. Then God appeared on my behalf to the terror of enemies, compared to an earthquake. Came—not by change of place, but by manifestation of presence and power. Brought into freedom and comfort: he ascribes all mercies to God’s good pleasure as the first spring. Righteousness—just cause; innocency toward Saul, from whose blood he kept his hands pure. Upright—thou metest the same measure he meteth to others; therefore mercy and truth to the merciful and true. Perfect—providence, though sometimes dark, always wise, just, unblameable; the truth of promises approved by innumerable experiences. Gentleness—clemency pardoning sins; grace and benignity. Heathen—transported beyond himself in relation to Christ his seed, by whom alone this is done, applied to the calling of the Gentiles. His king—the king God chose and anointed, and all his posterity, especially the Messiah, David’s seed.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Psalm 18)

reformed.quote: David came to the kingdom through almost insurmountable obstacles—fugitive under Saul, then harassed by tumults and foreign enemies to old age. These calamities he would never have surmounted without God’s power; he does not sing triumph to himself but magnifies God by lofty epithets. His reign was an image and type of Christ’s kingdom, victorious by the Father’s power despite the world’s resistance. Love to God is the principal part of true godliness; nothing he values more than free spontaneous love. Heaping titles fortifies faith: those God defends are surrounded by impregnable ramparts. He cried in distress and was heard from the temple; theophany similitudes confirm power and providence. Brought into a broad place because God delighted in him—good pleasure first. When he speaks of reward according to righteousness, both are needed: free election to the kingdom, and faithful obedience in the charge; God maintained his champion. With the merciful he shows himself merciful—yet hypocrites must not abuse prosperity. Victories prove the cause just under vocation, not cruelty. Enemies cried to Jehovah but he did not answer hypocrites who claimed his favor for injustice; he hears those who call in truth. Jehovah lives in the evidence of his works; great deliverances and forever mercy to David his anointed and his seed.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Book of Psalms (on Psalm 18)

verses.text: I love you, LORD, my strength.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Love—Most affectionately, and with my whole soul; as the Hebrew word signifies. David opens the song of deliverance with whole-souled love to the LORD his strength.

Love God with the whole heart as the first response to saving strength. Grace kindles affection; the hearer must still love the LORD who has been his strength, not treat deliverance as a trophy without devotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: love to God is the principal part of true godliness; there is no better way of serving God than to love him. He requires to possess all the affections of the heart. There is no sacrifice he values more than when we are bound to him by free and spontaneous love. David makes as it were a solemn vow: Lord, as thou art my strength, I will continue united and devoted to thee by unfeigned love.

Affectionate love answered to free goodness. Deliverance must not breed ingratitude; the heart stays bound to the Strength who saved.

verses.text: The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge; my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Rock—To which I flee for refuge, as the Israelites did to their rocks. Horn—It is a metaphor from those beasts whose strength lies in their horns. Fortress, deliverer, shield, and stronghold heap names for the God who shelters.

Take refuge in this many-named God. Grace supplies the rock; the hearer must still flee to him rather than invent another fortress.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David heaps titles to honor God because it is hard to keep mind and heart stayed in him. Those God intends to succor are surrounded by impregnable ramparts; though a thousand deaths appear, they ought not to fear. The design is to fortify faith so that whatever afflictions befall, we have recourse to God. I will trust in him.

God alone is complete armor. Multiple titles train the heart not to seek support elsewhere at the first temptation.

verses.text: I call on the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; and I am saved from my enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: calling on the LORD, who is worthy to be praised issues in being saved from enemies. Praise and petition belong together in the day of war.

Call on the praiseworthy LORD and expect rescue. Grace enables the cry; the hearer must still actually call rather than praise in theory while enemies go unanswered in prayer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: calling upon God here signifies recourse to him for protection and asking deliverance by prayer. Having said he trusted, David subjoins evidence of trust: every one who confides will earnestly beseech aid in need. He will be saved because he will have recourse to God. Prayers mingled with praises; remembrance of past grace animates free petition.

Trust proves itself in calling. Praise-woven prayer is faith’s evidence, not bare self-confidence.

verses.text: The cords of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Death—Dangerous and deadly troubles. Floods—Their multitude, and strength, and violent assaults, breaking in upon me like a flood. Cords and torrents name extremity, not mild inconvenience.

Name the danger honestly before God. Grace meets flood-level trouble; the hearer must still cry from within the cords rather than deny the waters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David recounts illustrious proofs that God’s hand is strong enough to repel dangers and calamities. Death is personified as a conqueror binding the vanquished. The torrents of destruction made him afraid—yet the narrative moves toward the God who hears.

Extremity is true, and so is the Helper. Faith does not minimize the flood; it recalls that God has already answered such distress.

verses.text: The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death came on me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Sorrows—Which brought me to the brink of the grave. Death—Had almost taken hold of me, before I was aware. Sheol’s cords and death’s snares press the same nearness to the end.

Own how near the snare came. Grace delivers from brink-of-grave sorrow; the rescued still remember how close entanglement felt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: cords of the grave and snares of death prevented him—nearly seized him. The psalm piles images so that later deliverance will look as great as the danger was.

Death’s snares are not rhetorical padding. Providence lets the faithful feel the brink that God’s later rescue will answer.

verses.text: In my distress I called on the LORD, and cried to my God. He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Temple—Out of his heavenly habitation. In distress he called; from the temple God heard, and the cry reached his ears.

Distress prayer reaches heaven’s temple. Grace opens the ear of God; the hearer must still cry for help rather than assume silence is piety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: in distress he called upon Jehovah and cried to his God; God heard from his temple, and the cry came into his ears. Recourse in trouble is the fruit of prior trust. Heaven’s temple is not deaf to the servant’s voice.

God hears from his dwelling. Answered cry is covenant faithfulness, not lucky coincidence in the storm.

verses.text: Then the earth shook and trembled. The foundations also of the mountains quaked and were shaken, because he was angry.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Then—Then God appeared on my behalf in a glorious manner, to the terror and confusion of all mine enemies, which is here compared to an earthquake. Anger shakes earth and mountain foundations.

God’s anger for his servant’s sake can rock the world-picture of the psalm. Grace delivers by holy wrath against oppressors; the hearer still trusts the God who appears, not a tame spectator.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David, unable to extol the aid enough, sets forth an image in sky and earth. Sudden changes awaken those asleep to a presiding God. The earthquake similitude removes doubt and confirms faith in power and providence; he does not narrate bare history but uses similitudes so slow minds may apprehend God by external signs.

Deliverance is God-sized. The quaking image teaches providence, not that every rescue must look like geology.

verses.text: Smoke went out of his nostrils. Consuming fire came out of his mouth. Coals were kindled by it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: There went, &c.—All these seem to be figurative expressions, denoting the greatness of his anger. Smoke, fire, and coals picture holy wrath, not human temper.

Take the figures as greatness of anger on the servant’s behalf. Grace confronts enemies with holy fire; the hearer must not shrink the God who saves into mere mildness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: smoke from nostrils and devouring fire mark God clothed in anger for his people’s deliverance. The imagery wakes dull hearts to the majesty that fights for the oppressed.

Figurative wrath is still opposition to the enemy. God is not a neutral referee when he delivers his own.

verses.text: He bowed the heavens also, and came down. Thick darkness was under his feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Bowed—By producing thick and dark clouds, whereby the heavens seem to come down to the earth. Came—Not by change of place, but by the manifestation of his presence and power on my behalf.

God “comes down” by manifested power, not relocation. Grace is presence-for-help; the hearer trusts the God who bows the heavens for the distressed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he bowed the heavens also, and came down. Thick darkness under his feet. God draws near in storm theophany so that deliverance is seen as his act.

Condescension without change of essence. The Most High manifests power on earth for his servant’s rescue.

verses.text: He rode on a cherub, and flew. Yes, he soared on the wings of the wind.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Cherub—Or, upon the cherubim, upon the angels, who are also called God’s chariots, upon which he is said to sit and ride. Not to be understood grossly, but to denote God’s using the ministry of angels in raising storms. Fly—As swiftly as the wind.

God’s swift help may use angelic ministry. Grace moves faster than the enemy’s plot; the hearer still looks to the Rider, not to secondary causes alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he rode upon a cherub and flew; carried on the wings of the wind. The psalm clothes providence in chariot imagery so faith sees speed and sovereignty in the rescue.

God acts swiftly from heaven. Secondary winds do not dethrone the God who rides them for his people’s sake.

verses.text: He made darkness his hiding place, his pavilion around him, darkness of waters, thick clouds of the skies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Darkness—He covered himself with dark clouds. Waters—Watery vapors. Covering and canopy hide and reveal at once the God who comes to save.

God may veil himself in dark waters even while acting. Grace is not always sunny clarity; the hearer still trusts the covered Majesty who fights for him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he made darkness his secret place; pavilion of dark waters and clouds. God is present in the storm-canopy that terrifies enemies and shelters purpose.

Hiddenness is not absence. Providence can work under thick cloud without ceasing to be for the servant.

verses.text: At the brightness before him his thick clouds passed, hailstones and coals of fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: At—His glorious and powerful appearance. Passed—Or, passed away, vanished, being dissolved into showers. Brightness breaks into hailstones and coals of fire.

Glory can erupt through the cloud in judgment-imagery. Grace for the servant may mean storm for the foe; hold both without softening either.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: at the brightness before him the clouds resolve into hail and coals of fire. Sudden changes give a livelier sense of God’s power than uniform course.

Brightness that breaks the cloud is still the same LORD. Deliverance-theophany is not random weather.

verses.text: The LORD also thundered in the sky. The Most High uttered his voice: hailstones and coals of fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s movement: thunder and the Most High’s voice continue the theophany—hailstones and coals again. Heaven speaks against the oppressors.

Hear the LORD’s voice in the deliverance. Grace thunders for the distressed; the hearer ascribes the peal to God, not chance sky.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Jehovah thundered; the thunder is the voice of God, not mere chance or nature independent of his will. David rises above phenomena to the supreme governor who launches thunderbolts as from his mouth.

Secondary causes do not erase the Speaker. The Most High’s voice is the meaning of the storm for faith.

verses.text: He sent out his arrows, and scattered them. He routed them with great lightning bolts.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Arrows—Lightnings. Them—Mine enemies. Arrows and lightnings scatter and rout the foes.

God’s weapons put enemies to flight. Grace fights; the rescued still give God the credit for the rout rather than their own arm alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: enemies scattered by the arrows of God—overthrown not by the hands of men alone but by God launching thunderbolts. Metaphorical language brings the slow to acknowledge God as author of deliverance.

Victory’s first cause is God. Human swords, if used, do not steal the glory of the lightning’s Lord.

verses.text: Then the channels of waters appeared. The foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, LORD, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Discovered—By mighty earthquakes, which overturned the earth, and made its lower parts visible. Channels of the sea and foundations laid bare at rebuke and blast of nostrils recall Red Sea-scale power.

Rebuke can bare the world’s foundations in the psalm’s imagery. Grace remembers covenant wonders; the hearer trusts the same rebuking breath that once made a path through waters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: sources of the waters seen alludes to the Red Sea miracle. Special benefits recall the covenant with the whole people, assuring that the God who split the sea still delivers his servant.

Personal rescue tied to covenant memory. The blast of nostrils is the LORD of the Exodus still acting.

verses.text: He sent from on high. He took me. He drew me out of many waters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: sent from on high, he took me; drew me out of many waters—personal snatch from the flood after the cosmic storm.

God reaches down and draws out. Grace is vertical rescue; the hearer still knows he was taken, not that he swam free by cleverness alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he sent from on high, took me, drew me from many waters. After the theophany, the point is personal: God himself extracts his servant from overwhelming flood.

Deliverance is from above. Many waters do not cancel election to be taken by God’s hand.

verses.text: He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me; for they were too mighty for me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s movement: rescued from the strong enemy and those who hated—because they were too mighty. Weakness confessed, strength located in God.

Admit foes too strong for you. Grace rescues the overmatched; the hearer must still cry rather than pretend parity with hatred.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: rescued from the strong enemy and haters too mighty for him. David’s victories are traced to God’s favor; the inequality of strength magnifies the Helper.

Overmatch is the stage for providence. God maintains his champion when human odds fail.

verses.text: They came on me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Prevented—They had almost surprized me. Confronted in the day of calamity, yet the LORD was support.

Calamity’s day can nearly ambush; God remains the support. Grace meets surprise attack; lean on the LORD when enemies arrive early.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they confronted in the day of calamity, but Jehovah was his support. Near-surprise does not mean God arrived late; support held when the day was darkest.

Support in calamity is covenant presence. Almost-surprised is still under the God who upholds.

verses.text: He brought me out also into a large place. He delivered me, because he delighted in me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Brought—Out of my straits and difficulties, into a state of freedom and comfort. So he ascribes all his mercies to God’s good pleasure, as the first spring of them.

Broad place and rescue because God delighted in him. Delight is favor; the hearer still receives freedom as gift rooted in God’s good pleasure—and answers with loyal love, not presumption that delight cannot be grieved by later unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: brought into a broad place because God delighted in him. A little before, blessings are traced to God’s good pleasure; election to the kingdom and free favor stand first. Deliverance flows from God’s delight, not from David inventing his own crown.

Broad place is the fruit of divine good pleasure. Rescue because he delighted grounds the servant in free grace before any talk of reward.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that God brought David into a broad place and rescued him because he delighted in him, and that mercies spring from God’s good pleasure. Readers in Wesley’s line stress ascribing all mercies to that good pleasure as first spring while still hearing delight as favor the servant must not presume upon by later departure. Calvin and those who follow him stress free good pleasure and delight as the electing fountain of the kingdom and of rescue—grace first, before integrity is even named.

verses.text: The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness. According to the cleanness of my hands, he has recompensed me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Righteousness—Just cause. The innocency of my actions towards Saul, from whose blood I kept my hands pure. Reward according to cleanness of hands is plea of integrity in the controversy, not claim to sinless perfection before God.

God deals according to a righteousness in the case—clean hands toward the enemy. Grace enabled that integrity; the hearer must still keep hands clean in conflict and may plead a just cause without claiming merit that buys salvation wholesale.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David seems to contradict tracing blessings to good pleasure, yet both are needed: God freely chose him king, and he yielded faithful obedience in the charge. God is like a combat president who chose his champion and then maintained him who performed the office faithfully. Aid fails not those who follow their calling within its limits. He does not varnish iniquity; he boasts of help given to an innocent man often near death.

Reward according to righteousness is God vindicating his called servant’s integrity in office and controversy—never a ladder of merit that replaces free election to the kingdom.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that the LORD dealt with David according to his righteousness and rewarded according to clean hands. Wesley hears a just-cause plea: innocence toward Saul and clean hands in the conflict, grace-enabled integrity one may plead without claiming absolute sinlessness. Reformed commentators hear the same vindication only after free good pleasure chose the king: God maintains his champion’s faithful calling—reward as covenant defense of integrity, not wages that purchased the throne.

verses.text: For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: kept the ways of the LORD; not wickedly departed from God. Integrity is continued adherence, not a single gesture.

Keep the ways; do not depart wickedly. Grace enables loyalty; the hearer must still refuse departure when pressure invites another path.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he kept Jehovah’s ways and did not wickedly depart from his God. Faithful performance of the charge committed to him—staying inside the call despite attempts to shake faith.

Perseverance in the assigned ways. Departure refused is obedience under a prior call, not self-made religion.

verses.text: For all his ordinances were before me. I didn’t put away his statutes from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Judgments—I diligently studied and considered them. Rules before him; statutes not put away—Word kept in view.

Keep God’s rules before you; do not shelve statutes. Grace supplies the Word; the hearer must still study and not put it away under temptation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: all his judgments were before me; statutes not put away. The servant keeps ordinances in sight as the path of the calling.

Both traditions affirm obedience that keeps God’s word before its eyes. Statutes retained are how integrity is walked, not optional ornament.

verses.text: I was also blameless with him. I kept myself from my iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Iniquity—From that sin which I was most inclined or tempted to. Blameless before him and kept from guilt names watched temptation, especially the lure to seize the kingdom violently against Saul.

Blamelessness here is self-keeping from a pressing guilt—grace-enabled restraint the servant practiced. The hearer must still keep himself from the sin that most beckons in his conflict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: upright with him and kept from his iniquity—integrity in the matter charged, under God’s eye. Not a denial that sinners need mercy, but a claim that in this controversy he had not turned aside into the guilt his enemies alleged or the shortcut temptation offered.

Blameless before him is sincerity in the calling under trial—God-ward integrity in the office, not a boast of impeccability that needs no Savior.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s refrain: so the LORD rewarded according to righteousness and clean hands in his sight—the vindication repeated after the integrity claim.

God sees clean hands and answers with reward in the controversy. Grace noticed the integrity; continue the clean-handed way rather than treat vindication as license.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: therefore Jehovah recompensed according to righteousness and cleanness before his eyes. The “therefore” ties reward to integrity in the combat God assigned—eyes of God, not flattering human courts.

His recompense comes under God’s sight. Vindication is judicial and covenantal, flowing from the God who already delighted to set him in the fight.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess the refrain: the LORD rewarded according to righteousness and cleanness of hands in his sight. Arminian readers stress that God answers lived integrity in the just cause—clean hands that must be kept. Reformed readers stress that this “therefore” still sits under prior good pleasure and calling: recompense is the Judge maintaining his servant, not the servant collecting wages that founded the relationship.

verses.text: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man, you will show yourself perfect.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Upright—Thou metest to every one the same measure, which he meteth out to others; and therefore thou wilt perform mercy and truth to those who are merciful and true to others.

With the merciful God shows himself merciful—moral symmetry that encourages mercy and blamelessness. Grace forms merciful people; they must still practice mercy expecting God’s like dealing, without turning the verse into a cold bargain that empties gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God, in delivering an innocent man, showed he is merciful toward the merciful and pure toward the pure. General doctrine: God does not disappoint his servants who wait with meekness; every one shall reap the fruit of his righteousness. Differ from hypocrites who abuse prosperity to claim divine favor while sacrificing to Fortune.

God’s dealing matches the servant’s way as moral government under grace—encouragement to integrity, not a marketplace that replaces mercy with earnings.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that with the merciful God shows himself merciful and with the blameless he shows himself blameless. Wesleyan interpreters hear measure for measure that urges merciful and true living toward others. Calvin hears the same moral correspondence as proof God favors integrity—and as general comfort that servants who wait meekly are not disappointed—without letting hypocrites turn success into a claim against heaven.

verses.text: With the pure, you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Pure—Free from the least mixture or appearance of unrighteousness, or unfaithfulness. Froward—Thou wilt cross him and walk contrary to him.

Purity met with purity; crookedness met with God’s opposing path. Grace warns the froward; straighten rather than force God to walk contrary to you.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: with the pure, pure; with the perverse, God shows himself perverse—strange wording to awaken hypocrites who sleep under judgment. Like Leviticus: if you walk contrary, I will walk contrary—obstinacy makes God harden himself to break them. Stubbornness gains a God who feels like iron against stone.

Opposition to the crooked is holy, not capricious. God may take a form of severity the perverse themselves provoke.

verses.text: For you will save the afflicted people, but the arrogant eyes you will bring down.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: save the humble; bring down haughty eyes. Deliverance has a moral tilt toward the lowly.

Humility saved, pride lowered. Grace lifts the humble; the hearer must still refuse haughty eyes that God promises to bring down.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: thou wilt save the afflicted/humble people and bring down haughty eyes. God’s pattern in David’s story: rescue for the low, humbling for confident pride.

Providence opposes haughty looks. Salvation of the humble is God’s settled way, not a mood.

verses.text: For you will light my lamp, LORD. My God will light up my darkness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Lightest—Given me safety, and comfort, and glory, and posterity also. God lights the lamp and lightens darkness.

Ask God to light your lamp in the dark. Grace is illumination and safety; do not curse the dark without seeking the LORD who lightens it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God lights the lamp—safety and continuance where darkness threatened extinction. The servant’s hope of light is located in “you” and “LORD. My God.”

Light comes from God alone. Darkness does not master the one whose lamp God lights.

verses.text: For by you, I advance through a troop. By my God, I leap over a wall.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Troop—Broken through the armed troops of mine enemies. Wall—I have scaled the walls of their strongest cities. By God: run against a troop; leap over a wall.

Feats of war credited to God. Grace enables the impossible push; the hearer still says “by you” and “by my God,” not “by my legend.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: by God he ran through a troop and leaped a wall—extraordinary enablement for God-assigned war. Strength for what flesh alone could not do.

Military success as divine enablement. The leap is gift, not proof of autonomous prowess.

verses.text: As for God, his way is perfect. The LORD’s word is tried. He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Perfect—His providence, though it may sometimes be dark, yet is always wise and just, and unblameable. Tried—The truth of God’s promises is approved by innumerable experiences. Shield for all who take refuge.

Trust the perfect way and tried word; take refuge under the shield. Grace invites refuge; actually hide in him when providence looks dark.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God’s way perfect; the word proves true; he is a shield to all who take refuge. After personal feats, the confession widens: this God’s path and promise hold for every truster.

Perfect way, proven word, universal offer of the shield to refuge-takers. Experience confirms what the mouth of God swore.

verses.text: For who is God, except the LORD? Who is a rock, besides our God,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Who—Our Lord is the only God, and therefore there is none that can hinder him from accomplishing his own work. Exclusive deity and rock.

Confess one God, one rock. Grace clears rivals; refuse other rocks that cannot save.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: who is God but Jehovah, and who a rock, besides our God? Monotheism as pastoral comfort: no rival can block his work for his people.

Exclusive God means unhindered purpose. The rhetorical questions shut the door on other saviors.

verses.text: the God who arms me with strength, and makes my way perfect?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Perfect—Perfectly plain and smooth, and clear from impediments. God equipped with strength and made the way blameless/smooth.

Strength and a cleared path are from God. Grace equips; walk the way he has made passable rather than invent another.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the God who girded with strength and made the way perfect/blameless. Enablement and path-clearing both from him who alone is rock.

Equipment and way are divine gifts. Blameless path here is God-made passage, not self-generated perfection.

verses.text: He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and sets me on my high places.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: High-places—Confirms me in that high estate into which he hath advanced me. Deer-feet and secure heights.

God gives sure footing in high places he assigned. Grace stabilizes advancement; do not climb heights God did not set.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: feet like hinds—unusual swiftness to climb inaccessible rocks; high places are strongholds taken by right of the war God authorized. Nothing seized as another man’s by private ambition.

Swift secure heights under calling. The deer-feet are gift for God-given fortresses.

verses.text: He teaches my hands to war, so that my arms bend a bow of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: trains hands for war; arms bend a bow of bronze—martial skill as tutelage from God.

Credit training and strength to God’s schooling. Grace teaches the hands; refuse to treat skill as self-made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: hands taught to war; arms strong enough for a bow of bronze/brass—dexterity not from mere practice but singular goodness. Something surpassing natural strength.

War-craft as secret virtue from God. Training is providence, not bare technique.

verses.text: You have also given me the shield of your salvation. Your right hand sustains me. Your gentleness has made me great.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Salvation—Thy protection, which hath been to me like a shield. Held—Kept me from falling into mischiefs enemies designed. Gentleness—Thy clemency, whereby thou hast pardoned my sins; thy grace and benignity.

Shield, right hand, and gentleness that made him great—clemency and pardon inside the warrior’s song. Grace is not only power; the hearer needs supporting gentleness and forgiven sin even while God makes him great.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: shield of thy salvation; right hand held him up; clemency/gentleness increased him—continuation of divine favor. Without God’s shield he would have taken deadly wounds; free goodness carried him forward in honor.

Salvation-shield and upholding right hand are free preservation. Greatness grows by God’s gentleness, not by raw force alone.

verses.text: You have enlarged my steps under me, My feet have not slipped.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Slipt—As they are apt to do in narrow and uneven ways. Wide place under steps; feet did not slip.

Ask for room underfoot so you do not slip. Grace widens the path; walk carefully still on what was once narrow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: enlarged steps—opened even pathway where there was no access; when reduced to distress with no escape, God brought him out. Feet did not stagger. Corrects distrust that trembles unless it sees a pleasant plain.

God’s office to enlarge and level ways. Unslipped feet are gift in former straits, not proof we never needed help.

verses.text: I will pursue my enemies, and overtake them. I won’t turn away until they are consumed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s movement: pursued, overtook, did not turn back till consumed—thoroughness in God-authorized pursuit.

Finish the conflict God assigned without quitting early. Grace strengthens pursuit; motives must stay under God’s command, not private cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: victories traced to God’s favor prove the cause good. David speaks as one executing judgment God committed—not bloodthirst, but vocation and pure zeal free of fleshly perturbation. As type of Christ, severity fell on the inflexibly obstinate.

David pursues his enemies under God’s warrant. Consumed enemies are God’s judgment through his servant, not a template for ungentle private revenge.

verses.text: I will strike them through, so that they will not be able to rise. They shall fall under my feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: thrust through; unable to rise; fell under feet—complete overthrow.

God can grant total defeat of oppressors. Grace decides the fall; do not glory in the thrust apart from the God who armed you.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: enemies made to sink; destruction of haters under God’s enabling. Effect shows God approved the servant’s cause.

Overthrow as token of divine favor on a just war. The fallen underfoot do not authorize sadism outside vocation.

verses.text: For you have armed me with strength to the battle. You have subdued under me those who rose up against me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s refrain of enablement: equipped with strength for battle; risers made to sink. God again named as the source.

“You equipped… you made.” Grace for the fight; keep attributing sinkage of foes to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: girded with strength for the war; enemies bowed under him. Insists the issue traces to God’s favor and thus to a just cause.

Battle strength is gift. Those who rise sink because God bowed them, not because fortune flipped.

verses.text: You have also made my enemies turn their backs to me, that I might cut off those who hate me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s movement: enemies turned backs; haters destroyed—rout and removal.

God can make enemies flee. Grace turns backs; destruction of hatred still asks clean hands in how victory is used.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: given the necks/backs of enemies; haters destroyed. God-authorized king, invincible by God’s power—type of Christ’s iron rod against the finally obstinate, while Christ also allures to repentance.

The rout of David’s enemies foreshadows the Messiah’s victory. David’s wars preview the kingdom that pardons the penitent and breaks the inflexible.

verses.text: They cried, but there was no one to save; even to the LORD, but he didn’t answer them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: they cried for help—none to save; cried to the LORD—he did not answer. Hypocrites’ prayers in extremity go unanswered.

Unanswered cry exposes false refuge in God while practicing injustice. Grace invites sincere calling; the hearer must not treat emergency piety as a substitute for repentance and truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they cried even to Jehovah, but he didn’t answer—hypocrites who abused God’s name by claiming his favor for unjust proceedings. Not that sincere callers are refused (Ps 145:18); they call with presumption, not truth, without changing purpose. Long prosperity made them seem God-backed while David cried in vain—until God cast them down.

God is nigh to all who call in truth; he is not bound to advance wicked enterprises dressed in prayer.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that the enemies cried for help and even to the LORD, yet he didn’t answer them. Arminian readers stress that emergency cries without turned lives are empty—sincere calling and amendment matter. Following Calvin, Reformed readers stress the same refusal as judgment on hypocrites who claimed God’s favor for injustice: not a denial that God hears truth-callers, but proof he will not underwrite wicked enterprises.

verses.text: Then I beat them small as the dust before the wind. I cast them out as the mire of the streets.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s image: beaten fine as dust; cast out like street mire—utter humiliation of the foe.

God can reduce oppressors to dust and mire. Grace decides the grinding; refuse to become mire-hearted in how you remember the win.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: beat them small as the dust before the wind; tread as mire. Continuation of God-given supremacy over false claimants to divine support.

The defeat is total, and it is God’s providence at work. Dust and mire language is judgment imagery, not a cue for perpetual spite.

verses.text: You have delivered me from the strivings of the people. You have made me the head of the nations. A people whom I have not known shall serve me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: People—From contentions and seditions under Saul, Ishbosheth, and Absalom. Heathens—Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, Syrians, and others. Not known—Even barbarous and remote nations. Delivered from strife; made head of nations.

God can quiet internal strife and set his servant over peoples unknown. Grace expands rule; stay servant of the LORD while heading nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: delivered from contentions of the people; made head of nations; unknown peoples serve. Domestic strife and foreign submission both from God’s hand.

David’s rule over nations comes to him as a gift. Headship over nations is providence on the anointed, previewing wider rule.

verses.text: As soon as they hear of me they shall obey me. The foreigners shall submit themselves to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Hear—As soon as they understand my will and pleasure, they shall instantly comply. Foreigners cringe at the hearing.

Reputation of God’s king can win obedience at a word. Grace spreads the name; do not confuse cringing fear with converted love—yet still thank God for subdued opposition.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: at the hearing of the ear they obey; foreigners feign submission from fear. Even half-hearted compliance shows God enlarging David’s sway.

Fame that subdues is God’s tool. Cringing may be fear not faith—and still serves the anointed’s security.

verses.text: The foreigners shall fade away, and shall come trembling out of their strongholds.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Close places—Out of their strong holds, where they shall lurk for fear of me. Lost heart; trembling from fortresses.

God can empty fortresses by fear. Grace breaks morale; the king still must not trust fear alone as if it were discipleship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: foreigners lose courage and tremble out of concealment. Strongholds fail when God melts hearts before his servant.

Foreigners lose heart even inside their strongholds. Lost heart is God’s doing against those who opposed his anointed.

verses.text: The LORD lives! Blessed be my rock. Exalted be the God of my salvation,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: The Lord—He and he only is the true living God. Blessed rock; exalted God of salvation.

Bless and exalt the living LORD. Grace that saved must end in doxology; refuse dead idols after living help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Jehovah lives—not mere bare essence, but life shown in works that preserve the world. Blessed be my strength; exalted the God of salvation. When God hides his working, the sense “God lives” fades from minds; when he shows power, praise rises.

Living God means active Savior. Blessing the rock is faith’s response to evident vital energy in deliverance.

verses.text: even the God who executes vengeance for me, and subdues peoples under me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s frame: God who gave vengeance and subdued peoples—vengeance as God’s gift, not private heat.

Ascribe vengeance and subdued peoples to God. Grace may grant just recompense; the heart must still refuse taking vengeance as a personal toy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God who gives vengeance and subdues peoples—victories attributed solely to him. Nothing but what God gave; power for what he could not have expected without confidence in aid.

Vengeance as divine gift through the office. Subdued peoples magnify the Giver, not the ego of the king.

verses.text: He rescues me from my enemies. Yes, you lift me up above those who rise up against me. You deliver me from the violent man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Violent man—From Saul: whom for honour’s sake he forbears to mention. Rescued, exalted above risers, delivered from the man of violence.

Name deliverance from violent men without needless dishonor. Grace lifts above aggressors; remember the Rescuer more than nursing the grudge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: deliverer from enemies; lifted above those who rose; delivered from the violent man. Epithets confirm God displays vital energy in government and rescue.

Exaltation over violent opposition is God’s act. The type points beyond Saul to every violence that cannot overthrow the anointed line.

verses.text: Therefore I will give thanks to you, LORD, among the nations, and will sing praises to your name.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Heathen—David is transported beyond himself, and speaks in special relation to Christ who was to be his seed, of whom he was an eminent type, and by whom alone this was done. Justly applied to Christ and the calling of the Gentiles (Rom 15:9).

Praise among the nations looks past David to Messiah’s Gentile mission. Grace widens the song; join the praise among the nations rather than keep salvation tribal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: therefore praise among the heathen and sing to the name. The thanksgiving expands to the nations—fitting the type of Christ’s kingdom victorious despite world resistance.

David’s praise is sung among the nations. Paul’s citation seals that David’s praise foresaw Gentile inclusion under the greater Son.

verses.text: He gives great deliverance to his king, and shows loving kindness to his anointed, to David and to his offspring, forever more.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: His king—To the king whom God himself chose and anointed, and to all his posterity; and especially to the Messiah, who is called David’s seed (Acts 13:23; Rom 1:3). Great salvation and steadfast love forever.

Covenant love to the anointed and offspring forever—centered in the Messiah. Grace keeps the promise; the hearer trusts forever-love in David’s greater Son and lives as one claimed by that steadfast love, not as if forever were a blank check for unfaithfulness without a Redeemer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: great deliverances for his king; mercy to David his anointed and to his seed forever. The psalm ends in covenant hesed to the royal line—image and type of Christ’s kingdom, always victorious by the Father’s power despite the world’s resistance.

Forever steadfast love is God’s oath to the anointed line fulfilled in Christ. Great salvation is covenant faithfulness, not uncertain mood.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess great salvation for the king and steadfast love to David’s anointed and offspring forever, reaching especially to the Messiah. Arminian commentators stress the forever promise focused in Christ the seed—covenant love that claims the hearer for loyal trust and praise among the nations. Calvin and those who follow him stress the same forever hesed as God’s invincible maintenance of the anointed kingdom typed in David and fulfilled in Christ—covenant loyalty secured by the Father’s power, not left hanging on the frailty of the earthly throne alone.
